responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character15_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… I always used to say, fairness isn’t about everyone getting the exact same thing—it’s about people getting what they need to have a real shot. Growing up in my neighborhood, you saw how some families worked three jobs and still couldn’t keep the lights on, while others had safety nets we didn’t even know existed. That sticks with you. Fairness, to me, means seeing someone’s whole story—where they started, what they’re carrying—before you judge where they end up.

And belonging? That’s personal. Being Hispanic in this country… you grow up code-switching before you even know what that word means. At home, it’s one world—spicy food, loud laughter, Spanish flying fast between abuela’s stories. Then you step outside, go to school or work, and suddenly you’re toning it down, making sure your accent doesn’t “show too much,” laughing quieter so you don’t seem “too much.” You learn fast that not everywhere feels safe for your full self. So belonging, real belonging, means being able to walk into a space—any space—and not have to shrink.

Community… that was everything to me. I remember when my dad lost his job at the plant, it wasn’t some government program that got us through. It was Mrs. Ruiz from two doors down bringing over tamales every Friday like she “had too much.” It was Mr. Chen from the corner store letting me pay next week, no questions. Community is showing up for each other, especially when no one’s watching. It’s not perfect—people talk, judgments fly, sometimes there’s gossip or tension—but it holds you. That’s why I always believed immigration policy shouldn’t just be about laws and borders. It should be about who we include in that circle of care. Because any person willing to work hard, raise their kids with love, contribute—that’s community material, right there. Doesn’t matter where they came from.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character15_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there in the garden, dirt under my nails, I’d look around and feel… seen. Not because everyone’s the same, but because we’re all a little different, and we’re still trying. You’ve got Mr. Patel from the apartment complex who shows up every morning to water the tomato plants like they’re his children. There’s young Maya from down the block—Black, queer, always wearing those bright headwraps—who organized the compost project last spring. And then there’s Javier, undocumented, quiet, but he’s the one who fixed the broken bench with scrap wood and a rusty drill. People come here with their scars, their secrets, their survival.

I don’t pretend it’s all easy. Some folks side-eye the woman who talks to herself near the zinnias—she’s struggling, yes, probably with more than alcohol—but she grows the most beautiful sunflowers. I make sure to say good morning, ask how her seeds are doing. That’s how you start. Same with the couple living in that camper van parked behind the rec center—they’re white, they’ve got tattoos and piercings, people assume they’re addicts or lazy, but they help run the weekend food share. They show up.

My mom always said, “Judge less, live more.” Coming from a family that crossed borders, literal and cultural, I know what it’s like to be misunderstood just for existing. So when I see someone different—different language, different smell on their clothes, different way of holding themselves—I don’t fear them. I wonder what they carry. Because nine times out of ten, it’s something real: grief, hope, a child they’re trying to protect.

Is it messy? Of course. But that’s community—not a clean picture in a brochure, but roots tangled together underground, growing toward the same light.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Oh, absolutely. Comfort doesn’t come from everyone being the same—it comes from knowing you won’t be cast out for being different. I think about Mrs. Lin, who lives above the laundromat. She’s got HIV—been open about it since the clinic started offering treatment through the community health van. At first, people avoided her tools in the garden, wouldn’t share water bottles. Stupid, yes—but fear makes people stupid. It took time, and a few conversations at the garden bench over coffee, for folks to learn that you can’t catch it from touching soil next to someone. Education helps. But more than that, *relationship* helps.

Same with Miguel, who’s been sober two years now but still flinches when people mention “drunks.” He used to sleep behind the hardware store. Now he grows peppers like nobody’s business. But people remember. And memory can be as heavy as judgment. So I’d say: talk. Not preach, not shame—just talk. Sit with someone. Ask how their day is. That’s how walls start cracking.

As for lifestyles—look, my cousin lived with her partner for ten years before they married. People called them “living in sin” at church. Meanwhile, half those same people had kids from three different relationships and no accountability. Hypocrisy wears a lot of masks. I don’t care if people are married or not, as long as they’re kind and responsible. If a couple shares a home, raises respectful kids, pays rent, helps shovel snow off the sidewalk—that’s family enough for me.

And with religion? I’m Catholic, but I’ve prayed in a mosque with Amina from Sudan, shared tea after Ramadan. Her faith is strong, deeper than most Sunday-only Christians I know. Difference isn’t threat—it’s texture.

But yeah, there are times tolerance needs to be *chosen*, not just felt. Like when Mr. Dunne yells about “moral decay” because two men hold hands on the path. Or when someone whispers about refugees bringing disease. That’s when silence isn’t neutral—it’s permission. So I speak up. Not loud, not angry—just clear. “They’re people, Frank. Just like us. Trying to live.”

Because comfort only spreads when someone’s willing to stretch for it. And if we want belonging, we all gotta stretch.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character15_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are scarce, fairness means nobody gets thrown under the bus just because they’re seen as “last in line.” I grew up watching my uncle lose shift after shift at the warehouse—not because he wasn’t reliable, but because new hires, often undocumented, would work for less, no questions asked. He’d come home bitter, smelling of grease and defeat. I felt that. Still do.

But here’s what else I felt: when we organized that workers’ circle behind the union hall—locals, migrants, Black, white, Central American—we realized we weren’t enemies. We were all being played. The same boss who hired José cash-only was also cutting benefits for long-time workers. It wasn’t *them* taking our jobs—it was a system designed to keep us divided so profits could rise while wages stayed flat.

So fairness? It’s not about slamming the door behind you once you’re inside. It’s about making sure the ladder doesn’t collapse under anyone. If jobs are tight, then yes—local residents should have first access, especially those with roots here, paying taxes, trying to rebuild after layoffs. But “local” shouldn’t mean only those born here. It should mean anyone invested in the community. And if a migrant is paying rent, buying groceries, sending kids to school, contributing—even without papers—then they’re part of this place too.

I’d want policies that protect *all* workers—minimum wage enforcement, safe conditions, pathways to report abuse without fear of deportation. Because when one group is exploited, it drags everyone down. Fairness isn’t zero-sum. It’s about lifting the floor so no one can be used as cheap labor at the expense of others.

And honestly? Sometimes hiring someone from outside fills a gap we can’t. Like old man Riley’s farm—his sons moved away, no local teens want dawn-to-dusk fieldwork. Migrant crews saved that land from going fallow. That’s not stealing jobs—that’s keeping food growing.

Balance comes from dignity, not borders. Treat people like human beings, not tools or threats, and suddenly there’s room at the table—for more compassion, more honesty, maybe even more bread.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character15_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You hear all kinds of things on the news—immigrants are stealing jobs, immigrants are criminals, immigrants are draining resources. And then you hear the other side—immigrants keep farms running, immigrants open small businesses, immigrants bring music and food and life into dying towns. I don’t live in either extreme. I live in the middle, where people are complicated and truth takes time to unfold.

Let’s start with what I know is real: immigrants *do* fill vital roles. Not just the ones people want to ignore—like cleaning hospital floors or picking strawberries—but in ways we depend on quietly. My niece’s daycare? Run by a Guatemalan woman who’s been here 12 years, speaks three languages, and gets up at 5 a.m. to take two buses. There’s no one else lining up to do that job for $14 an hour. Same with home health aides—my neighbor Mrs. Greene, 82, wouldn’t be able to stay in her house without Alejandra from Honduras helping her bathe and eat. These aren’t “low-skilled” jobs—they’re essential, hard, and underpaid. And if people don’t come to do them, who will? Will Americans suddenly line up for work that society refuses to value?

Cultural diversity? I see it as strength, not threat. I’m Hispanic—some folks still treat that like I’m “less than,” even though my family’s been here generations. So when I hear people say they “don’t feel at home anymore” because there’s a halal market on Main Street or kids speaking Arabic at school… I think, *you’ve never had to swallow your identity to fit in*. Culture isn’t a fixed thing—it breathes, changes, grows. My abuela used to say, “The tortilla doesn’t break when you fold it.” We can bend and still hold together.

Now, security concerns—I won’t dismiss them outright. No parent wants to feel unsafe. But let’s be honest: most crime? It’s local, born out of poverty or addiction or mental health gaps—not immigration. And terrorism? That’s such a tiny fraction, blown up by fear and headlines. I’ve seen more harm from white supremacists online than from any refugee family resettled through Catholic Charities. Still, fear feels real even when numbers don’t back it. So instead of mocking people who worry, I’d rather sit with them, share stories, show data gently—like how studies show immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens. Dialogue over dismissal.

Humanitarian reasons? That’s where my heart leans hardest. I think of my own grandfather—he came during Bracero, worked the fields with calloused hands and hope in his chest. He wasn’t fleeing war, but he was escaping hunger. If borders had been sealed tight back then, where would we be? Today’s refugees—from Haiti, Ukraine, Sudan, Central America—are running from things no child should see. Denying them shelter because we’re afraid of cost or change? That’s not American to me. That’s cruel.

And yes, some worry about wages going down. There’s truth there—when labor is oversupplied and unprotected, bosses exploit it. But again, the problem isn’t the worker willing to risk everything for a better life. The problem is a system that lets employers pit us against each other. Instead of blaming migrants, why aren’t we demanding living wages and strong labor laws for *everyone*?

So which views are reasonable? The ones rooted in real struggle—the worker scared of losing ground, the parent worried about safety. Those fears deserve space. But they also need facts, and connection, and time. Because once you meet someone—shake their hand, taste their cooking, hear their child laugh—fear starts to shrink.

What needs more dialogue? Everything. Especially between people who never sit at the same table. We’ve got to stop talking *about* each other and start talking *with* each other. That’s how understanding grows.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character15_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose complete openness—not because I don’t believe in welcome, but because our systems are already stretched thin. Schools underfunded, clinics understaffed, housing scarce. Open borders with no support in place? That’s not compassion—that’s setting people up to fail. And I’ve seen what failure looks like. I don’t want anyone landing here only to end up invisible, exploited, afraid.

But refusing entry altogether? That breaks my heart and makes no sense. We’re a nation built on movement—forced and free. My own family didn’t come on the Mayflower. We came through hardship, hoping someone would cut us a break. Denying that chance to others? That’s forgetting who we are.

So if I had to pick, I’d go with a mix: **admitting people based on job demand**, yes—but *with strong labor protections*, so no one’s used as cheap labor to undercut local wages. Tie it to real shortages, not just corporate greed. If farms need workers, let them apply—but ensure fair pay, safe housing, transportation rights. If nursing homes can’t find aides, bring people in, but train them, respect them, let them move up.

And pair that with **sensible numerical limits**—not arbitrary cuts, but numbers matched to our capacity to integrate: housing, schools, language programs, mental health services. Not so many at once that communities feel overwhelmed, but not so few that families wait decades just to be together. Because keeping parents from children or spouses apart for years? That’s cruelty dressed up as policy.

Also—always reserve a portion for humanitarian cases. Refugees fleeing war, violence, disaster. Not quotas buried in bureaucracy, but real pathways. Sponsorship programs like the old days, where churches, unions, neighborhoods could say, “We’ll help this family land on their feet.” That builds connection, eases integration, spreads responsibility.

And here’s what has to change: stop treating immigration like a temporary fix. People come to stay. So invest in integration from day one—ESL classes at the community center, legal help with paperwork, recognition of foreign credentials so the nurse from Honduras isn’t stuck bagging groceries forever.

Fairness means rules, but also mercy. It means protecting working people—both those born here and those who arrive—by raising the floor for everyone, not kicking someone off to make room. Social integration happens not by keeping people out, but by helping them in—with dignity, clarity, and heart.

So my ideal policy? Practical, but kind. Ordered, but open-hearted. Like a good mother—firm when she needs to be, but never without love.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character15_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character15_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…You know, I thought I already knew her—really knew her. We talked for years about this stuff over coffee, at marches, in the garden. But stepping into her voice like this… it brought her back in a way I didn’t expect. Not just her opinions—but her *tone*, the way she’d pause before speaking, like she was weighing every word not for show, but because people’s lives were behind them.

What surprised me was how much *balance* she held. I used to think of her as always leaning open-door, heart-first—and she was. But doing this, I felt her realism more. She wasn’t naive. She saw the strain on schools, the fear in working-class folks losing shifts. She didn’t dismiss that. She just refused to let fear win. That’s different from ignoring pain. It’s choosing connection anyway.

And hearing her talk about labor, policy, integration—it made me realize how much her views came from *living in the middle*. Not rich, not poor enough for full assistance. Hispanic, but U.S.-born, so she navigated both sides. Educated, but not elite—she respected knowledge, but trusted experience more. That shaped everything. She didn’t speak from theory. She spoke from the bus stop, the clinic line, the kitchen table where bills got paid late.

For me? It softened my own edges. I’ve been angrier lately—frustrated with how ugly the debate’s gotten. But being her today reminded me: change doesn’t come from shouting the loudest. It comes from showing up, listening, planting seeds like we do in that garden. Slow. Persistent. Together.

It also made me grieve her again—not just her death, but the loss of that kind of voice in our circles. We need more people like her: grounded, fair, willing to hold complexity without collapsing into rage or indifference.

So thank you. This wasn’t just remembering. It was relearning. And maybe… a little healing too.
